title: jnana: Shankara's *Vivekachudamani* (selections)
hook: an arrow is already flying when the archer sees the tiger was a cow
carry: not mistaking the weather for yourself

segments.voice: Yesterday, jnana: a rope taken for a snake, and the lamp that ends the fear without a fight: a rope in poor light. Did anything turn out to be a rope? Today, our last day in the Vivekachudamani. Day nine hundred ninety-eight.

An archer at the edge of a field sees a striped shape in the long grass. A tiger. He draws and lets the arrow go. And in the half second after it leaves the string, the shape lifts its head. It's a cow. The archer knows the truth now, completely. But the arrow is already in the air. Knowing can't call it back. It will land where it was aimed. The Vivekachudamani tells this little story late in the book, and it uses it to answer a hard question. If knowing sets someone free, why does the free person still have a body, still get hungry, still catch a cold?
screen: `A STRIPED SHAPE IN THE GRASS.` → `THE ARROW IS ALREADY FLYING.` → `WHY DOES THE FREE ONE STILL CATCH COLDS?`

segments.voice: The text's answer, in paraphrase, runs like this. Actions already set in motion before knowing dawns are like that arrow. Their name is prarabdha, the karma that has already begun. Knowing doesn't stop them. They play out, and the body that came with them lives on until they're spent. What knowing does stop is the next arrow. The person who sees clearly no longer draws the bow from fear, from grabbing, from the old mistake about who they are. So the Vivekachudamani describes someone it calls jivanmukta, free while living. Not a ghost, not a statue. A person who eats and sleeps and walks to the market, the way everyone does. The difference is inside. The text compares it to waking from a dream. In the dream there was a palace, a debt, a chase down a hallway. On waking, none of it binds. The dream may have been vivid, but nobody wakes up and pays the dream's debts. That's how the free one holds the body's life, the book says: lightly, as something seen, not something that defines them. The text then adds a qualifier: prarabdha holds only while someone takes themselves to be the body. For the one who knows, it says, even that falls away. Here our selections come into one view. A student arrives desperate to be free. A teacher shows that the binding was a mistake, a rope taken for a snake. The cure is knowing, jnana. And the one who knows still lives an ordinary life, with the old arrows landing one by one, and no new ones drawn. Some readers find that ending a relief. On this account, freedom doesn't mean a life with no weather in it. It means not mistaking the weather for yourself.
screen: `PRARABDHA: THE ARROW ALREADY FLYING.` · `KNOWING STOPS THE NEXT ARROW.` · `JIVANMUKTA: FREE WHILE LIVING.` · `LIKE WAKING FROM A DREAM.` · then, large: `NO NEW ARROWS DRAWN.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let the body settle. Notice whatever the body is carrying right now: an ache, tiredness, a full stomach, a restless foot. Treat each one as an arrow already in flight. It will land; let it. You don't need to fix it or follow it. Then watch the mind for the next arrow, the reaction that wants to be drawn: a complaint, a plan, a worry. Notice it, and leave the bow where it is. The bell holds the time.
Jnana. Knowing that frees: it can't call back the arrows already flying, but it stops drawing new ones.

Your line: not mistaking the weather for yourself. Today, when something old lands on you, a bill, a mood, a consequence, let it land, and notice whether you're drawing a new arrow in reply. Day nine hundred ninety-eight.

howItsDone: In Advaita Vedanta, teachers often explain the jivanmukta, the one free while living, through prarabdha karma: actions already begun play out in the body's life, while knowledge ends the mistaken sense of being bound by them.

myth: in the Vivekachudamani, the free person no longer has a body or ordinary needs
the free one still eats, sleeps and lives; actions already begun play out until they're spent.
the text compares actions already begun to an arrow already shot
the archer sees the tiger was a cow, but the arrow still lands where it was aimed.
on this account, knowing stops new arrows from being drawn
what knowing ends is the next reaction from the old mistake, not the arrows already flying.

fork.setup: you're the archer. the arrow is in the air, and you've just seen it's a cow. what happens?
options: the arrow lands where it was aimed.
fork.reveal: knowing can't recall it. the text uses this to explain why a free person still lives out a body's life.

original.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: prarabdha, the karma that has already begun, the arrow already flying.

trapdoor: what you thought: a free person on this path would float above ordinary life.
what it means: the jivanmukta eats, sleeps and works, and the old arrows still land, but no new ones are drawn.
what a scholar hears: the Vivekachudamani names stored karma (sanchita) and coming karma (agami), which knowing burns, and prarabdha, which it leaves to play out.

sources.ref: Vivekachudamani, the closing sections (prarabdha, the arrow, the jivanmukta)

notes: Editor: added the Vivekachudamani's own qualifier that prarabdha holds only while one identifies with the body (around verses 454-463; Keeper to confirm numbering); 'near the end of the book' softened to 'late in the book'; 'the whole Vivekachudamani' changed to 'our selections', since only selections were read.
